vignette:
Clara is a 42-year-old project manager who came to therapy at her husband’s urging, though she admits she has felt “off” for nearly two years now. She is soft-spoken but precise in her language, a quality she says she developed managing complex construction timelines. She sits forward in her chair, hands clasped, as if bracing for a deadline meeting.

Two years ago, Clara was diagnosed with a rare, aggressive form of bacterial meningitis. She remembers the day vividly—not the diagnosis itself, but the moment before. She had been in a conference room, presenting a quarterly budget to executives. Mid-sentence, a searing headache bloomed behind her left eye. She finished the presentation, drove herself home, and collapsed in the bathroom. Her husband found her on the floor, delirious and unable to speak. She spent eleven days in the ICU.

Clara does not remember most of those days. What she remembers, with excruciating clarity, is the night before she was intubated. A resident came in to explain the risks: stroke, brain damage, death. Clara’s husband was crying. She remembers thinking, I have to stay calm for him. She signed the consent form with a hand that would not stop shaking. That night, alone in the dark, she felt her body give way. She was certain she would not wake up.

But she did. She recovered fully, physically. Her doctors called her a miracle. Her husband wept with relief. Her colleagues sent flowers. Clara returned to work after three months, eager to feel normal again. But normal would not return.

At first, Clara attributed the changes to lingering fatigue. She had trouble concentrating, which was alarming for someone who once managed twelve subcontractors from memory. She began avoiding the breakroom because someone had left a half-empty cup of coffee there, and the smell reminded her of the hospital’s burnt Folgers. She stopped taking the elevator because the enclosed space made her chest tighten. She started driving to work an hour early to avoid traffic, because being trapped in a line of cars made her feel like she could not breathe.

Her husband noticed she no longer watched medical dramas, though she used to love them. She stopped going to the gym because the fluorescent lights were too bright, too white, too clinical. She began checking her temperature three times a day. Every headache, every stiff neck, sent her into a spiral. She has been to the emergency room four times in the past year for what turned out to be tension headaches and allergies. Each time, the doctors tell her she is fine. Each time, she does not believe them.

At work, Clara is still competent, but she is brittle. She micromanages her teams now, double-checking every detail, because she cannot tolerate uncertainty. She has stopped delegating. She works late, often until nine or ten, because the quiet of the empty office is the only time she feels safe. But even then, her mind wanders. She will be reviewing a budget and suddenly she is back in that hospital bed, the beeping of the monitors syncing with her heartbeat. She has to grip her desk to remind herself she is here, not there.

She has not told anyone this, but she has started rehearsing her own obituary. She does it in the shower, in the car, before falling asleep. She imagines what people would say, what her son would remember. She knows this is morbid, but she cannot stop. It feels like preparation, like a project plan for the worst-case scenario.

Clara’s husband tells her she is not the same person. He says it gently, with worry. She agrees. She feels like a stranger in her own life, waiting for the other shoe to drop, waiting for her body to betray her again. She is not afraid of death, she says. She is afraid of the moment just before—the terror of knowing it is coming, and being completely alone.
